meta.audience: Readers of the record of Zeniff
meta.location: The land of Lehi-Nephi and Shilom

world_behind.title: The enemy's case, stated in full
world_behind.text: Verses 12 through 17 give the Lamanite grievance narrative point by point, five complaints in chronological order, ending with the charge that a younger brother stole the records and seized the rule. Every item corresponds to an episode the reader has already read from Nephi's side, and none of the five is disputed on the facts.

world_behind.title: An appearance described
world_behind.text: Shaved heads, naked, a leathern girdle about the loins, armed with bows, arrows, swords, cimeters, stones, and slings. The girdle is what Elijah wore and what John the Baptist wore. The record is describing a military dress it expects its reader to be able to picture.

world_behind.title: Women's work, named
world_behind.text: Verse 5 is the record's only account of what the women of a colony did: spin, toil, work, and make fine linen and cloth of every kind. It sits in a verse about prosperity, and the verse presents it as part of the reason the prosperity existed.

world_behind.title: Everyone who could hold a weapon
world_behind.text: Old men able to bear arms and young men able to bear arms, placed in ranks by age; women and children hidden in the wilderness. This is a small colony emptying itself into a line of battle, and the king in it is old enough to remark on his own age.

world_behind.title: "The tradition of their fathers."
world_behind.text: The record's standing term for received belief. It occurs twenty-one times, nearly all in Alma. Zeniff uses it here to introduce the fullest statement of what that tradition actually contained, the only place the record spells it out.

world_behind.title: A sign-off closes the document
world_behind.text: Verse 22 confers the kingdom, says "I say no more," and blesses the people. Zeniff signs off the way the small-plates keepers did, and the next chapter opens in somebody else's voice.

words.text: Without warning. Zeniff sets guards specifically so it cannot happen again, which tells the reader it had happened before. The word marks the change in him between chapters: the man who trusted a treaty now runs a perimeter.

The word Zeniff used for what he wanted, and the word Limhi used when explaining to a nation in chains how it got there. Here it is neither a motive nor a charge but a report: they did inherit the land of their fathers, "for the space of twenty and two years" (v. 3). That is what the inheritance came to, and Zeniff is the one who writes the number down.

cites.quote: for the space of twenty and two years

spans.text: for the space of twenty and two years

words.text: Ordered lines, a military formation. Men are placed "every man according to his age," an organizing principle. The detail suggests a militia being arranged by the only criterion a farming colony had available.

The King James Bible spells it without the hyphen and has it once, at Proverbs 29:10. It enters this record with Enos, who used it of the Lamanites, and Zeniff uses it twice. Once here, of the same people. Once in the previous chapter, of his own commander, the man who ordered him killed for arguing that the two nations should make a treaty. No other writer in the record aims it at a Nephite.

Fiercely angry, and the word carries a sense of grievance. Three times in three verses, once for each stage of the journey, it structures the whole Lamanite complaint: wroth in the wilderness, wroth on the water, wroth in the promised land.

The King James word for killing on a battlefield scale, without approval or condemnation attached. Zeniff reports a great one and then says they did not number the dead, the opposite of what he did in the previous chapter, where he counted both sides.

phrases.term: I did cause that the women should spin, and toil, and work, and work all manner of fine linen
phrases.text: Four verbs, one of them repeated, and the products named. The record almost never says what women did; here it says, and puts the answer inside the sentence that reports the colony prospering. Clothing is the stated purpose: "that we might clothe our nakedness."

phrases.term: They had their heads shaved that they were naked
phrases.text: Reported as a fact about an army, in the middle of a weapons list. It matches what Enos said of the same people two centuries earlier, so the description is a tradition of long standing in this record.

phrases.term: I, even I, in my old age, did go up to battle against the Lamanites
phrases.text: Two intensifiers and a concession. Zeniff has already sent the women and children into the wilderness and drawn up every man who can carry a weapon; the sentence puts him in the line with them. He is writing this near the end of his life.

phrases.term: The Lamanites knew nothing concerning the Lord... therefore they depended upon their own strength
phrases.text: The explanation offered for the enemy's confidence, and it is not contemptuous. The next clause grants that they were a strong people as to the strength of men. Zeniff is distinguishing between two kinds of strength rather than denying they had one.

phrases.term: Believing in the tradition of their fathers, which is this
phrases.text: The phrase that introduces the list. Zeniff is about to recite his enemies' account of history in their own terms, and the colon does work no other verse in the record does. What follows is not his view and he does not mark where it stops. The second item is the reader's own story told back with the verdict reversed: "they were wronged in the wilderness by their brethren" (v. 12). Nephi's record has the same journey, the same brothers, and a different assignment of fault. The chapter lets the two versions stand next to each other without settling it.

cites.quote: they were wronged in the wilderness by their brethren

spans.text: they were wronged in the wilderness by their brethren

phrases.term: Because that Nephi was more faithful in keeping the commandments of the Lord
phrases.text: Zeniff breaking into his own recitation to supply the actual reason. The grievance list says Nephi took the lead; this clause says why he was given it. It is the one place the narrator's voice is audible inside the enemy's account.

phrases.term: They understood not the dealings of the Lord
phrases.text: The diagnosis of the anger, stated once and not repeated: incomprehension. It is the most sympathetic sentence anyone in this record writes about the Lamanites' original quarrel.

phrases.term: They said that he robbed them
phrases.text: The charge over the brass plates, which is the one grievance with a physical object at the center of it. Nephi took the records into the wilderness at the Lord's command; the other family called it theft. Both accounts agree on what happened and disagree on what to call it.

phrases.term: Thus they have taught their children that they should hate them
phrases.text: The mechanism by which a quarrel becomes a nation's inheritance. Verse 17 is about transmission, not about the original wrong: taught to hate, to murder, to rob, to plunder, and to destroy. The word for the result is eternal hatred, and it appears once more in the record.

phrases.term: His cunning, and lying craftiness, and his fair promises, deceived me
phrases.text: Zeniff's own admission, placed at the end of the enemy's grievance list rather than at the start of it. He has just explained why the Lamanites hate his people; then he says the hatred was used against him personally, and that he walked into it.

phrases.term: I did stimulate them to go to battle with their might
phrases.text: The verb occurs once in scripture. What Zeniff stimulated them with was the account in verses 12 through 18. He told his people the enemy's own version of history and then sent them out to fight. It is an unusual thing to use as a rallying speech.

phrases.term: I say no more. And may the Lord bless my people
phrases.text: The kingdom conferred, the record closed, and a blessing. Zeniff ends on his people, and the last thing in a document full of his own mistakes is a wish for the people those mistakes cost.

verses.label: v. 8
verses.title: A prophet's belt in a battle report
verses.text: The listing of bows, arrows, swords, cimeters, stones and slings breaks off for dress: the Lamanites "were girded with a leathern girdle about their loins." Only one other man in scripture wears that belt, John the Baptist at Matthew 3:4. The record pauses an order of battle to note what the enemy had on.

verses.label: v. 9–10
verses.title: The muster is defined at both ends of a life
verses.text: Old men that could bear arms and young men that were able, ranked "every man according to his age." Then Zeniff writes himself into the category he has just drawn, going up to battle in his own old age. The record has its narrator qualify under his own criterion, and does not remark on it.

verses.label: v. 12–13
verses.title: The grievance is set out in the plaintiff's vocabulary
verses.text: The word wronged lands three times across the pair: wronged in the wilderness, wronged crossing the sea, wronged in the land of their first inheritance, all of it running back to being driven out of Jerusalem. Zeniff states the Lamanite case as a list of injuries, in the terms its holders would use, before he answers a word of it.

verses.label: v. 14–16
verses.title: The same episodes return with their causes attached
verses.text: Verses 14, 15 and 16 each open with "and again" and each retells an item from the list, now with a reason the first telling withheld: a failure to understand, a hardened heart, a complaint about who was ruling whom. The record runs one sequence of events twice, once as complaint and once as explanation, and leaves the comparison to the reader.

chapter.title: The record publishes its enemy's case
chapter.text: Six verses of Lamanite grievance, listed in order, with no rebuttal attached to most of it. A national scripture giving the other side's account of its own founding is rare, and this one does it without softening the charges, including the charge that its founder was a thief.

chapter.title: The same events, two verdicts
chapter.text: Every grievance in the list corresponds to something the reader has already read. The facts are not disputed; the interpretation is. What the chapter shows is two peoples who agree entirely about what happened and cannot agree about what it meant.

chapter.title: The anger is diagnosed as incomprehension
chapter.text: Verse 14 says they were wroth because they understood not the dealings of the Lord. That is a different explanation than wickedness, and the record has given the other one often enough that this one stands out.

chapter.title: A quarrel between brothers becomes a national inheritance
chapter.text: The original dispute involved four men on one journey. Verse 17 accounts for how it reached the fourth century after them, and the account is entirely about what one generation deliberately handed to the next. Nothing in it is presented as innate.

chapter.title: Zeniff indicts himself inside the enemy's indictment
chapter.text: The grievance list ends with his own admission that Laman's fair promises deceived him and that his people have suffered for it. He does not use the enemy's history as an excuse; he uses it as context for his own error.

chapter.title: What he sent them out with was the truth about the other side
chapter.text: Nothing in verse 19 flatters his own people or asserts their cause. Zeniff had just finished reciting his enemies' grievances and his own error, and that recital is what he offered as preparation. It is an unusual thing to steady an army with.

chapter.title: The document ends without resolution
chapter.text: No deliverance, no prophecy, no reversal. A war won, flocks tended, a son crowned, and a blessing. The reader already knows from Mosiah 7 that the son is Noah and what comes next. The quiet ending is the darkest thing in the chapter.

applications.title: Learn to state the other case
applications.text: Zeniff could recite his enemy's grievances in their own terms and in order. Take a conflict you are inside and write the other party's account so accurately that they would sign it.

applications.title: Ask whether the facts are even in dispute
applications.text: Both sides agreed Nephi took the records; they disagreed about whether it was theft. Most stubborn conflicts are like that. Separate what happened from what it is being called.

applications.title: Consider incomprehension before malice
applications.text: The record's explanation for the founding anger is that they did not understand. Before assigning bad motives, spend the effort to check whether the person simply does not see what you see.

applications.title: Notice what you are teaching your children to feel
applications.text: Hatred here is inherited because it was taught. Ask what attitude toward some group your children are absorbing from you without anyone naming it.

applications.title: Name your own deception without excusing it
applications.text: Zeniff says he was deceived and that his people suffered for it, and offers no defense. Do the same about a decision of yours that cost other people something.

applications.title: Tell them the truth before the hard thing
applications.text: What he used to steady his people was an honest account. Try that with a group you are leading into something difficult.

questions.text: Could I state the case against me as well as the person making it?
Whose anger have I written off as malice when it might be confusion?
What am I calling by a name the other party would reject, and are we actually disagreeing about the facts?
What resentment did I inherit rather than form?
What went wrong because I believed a fair promise I wanted to believe?
If I closed my record today, would the last line be about me or about the people I was responsible for?
